I don't necessarily agree with the logic, but as someone who doesn't smoke marijuana, doubt I would even if it was fully legalized in my state, and generally runs with a more conservative crowd I think I can explain the logic. It's not as power conspiracy laced as some comments here would have you believe.

The status quo is that marijuana is illegal. Decades of fear mongering have ingrained in a sizable portion of the population with unrealistic ideas of the level of corruption marijuana will bring. Lots of people are of course coming around to the notion that they're simply not true. But it takes time to deprogram everyone.

The loudest remaining opposition are groups that say, "Well even if cannabis products aren't really any more dangerous than cigarettes or alcohol or other things we let adults choose to use responsibly if they so want - THINK OF THE CHILDREN, WON'T SOMEBODY PLEASE THINK OF THE CHILDREN!" And there is some probably irrational (I personally doubt it, but I'm no expert) logic that if you legalize cannabis for adult consumption suddenly the schools are gonna flooded with black market weed that wouldn't get there otherwise and the implication that otherwise good, straight A kids are gonna get hoodwinked and throw their lives away.

Again I don't personally think this is rational, but it's a belief that isn't entirely rare because of so many years of anti-marijuana rhetoric.

So legalization advocates decide to take an incremental victory and throw out strict regulations to appease the fearful. They can say if they limit the amount of marijuana anyone can legally purchase or be in possession of at one time it makes buying it from legal sources and then reselling it on a black market to minors inefficient & unprofitable so that eliminates that risk.

The same argument is applied to neighboring states. If neighbor states anti-cannabis advocacy groups are told, "Look, no one is going to be able to have more than an ounce at a time, it's not a working business model to buy it retail in our state and smuggle it to a black market in yours," it possibly makes them less likely to invest anything in an anti-legalization movement.

I don't think many people who really want legal recreational cannabis see a need for limits, but they take a pragmatic stance and say, "Well an ounce is a lot. I''ll accept that after I go through an ounce I have to go buy more if it shuts the fear mongers up and helps let it be legal at all."

On some level the taxation comes in, but that's really more in the number of plants you can possess personally. Even if you could buy 20 pounds of weed legally retail, if I'm paying all the tax on my legal purchase it's not easy to make a super effective business model to resell it tax free. There might exist some model. For example I could go to the price club and buy a dozen cases of soda and then resell the cans individually on the beach and probably make some money on the mark-up. People do that kind of thing all the time. In theory they're supposed to pay a tax on money earned doing so, but I'm sure many don't and/or under report earnings in a cash business. But it's such a small piece of the pie it's not worth dragneting everyone selling cans of cola on the beach for tax evasion. The same logic could be applied to a theoretical weed re-seller. It would be small potatoes for that to be the motive. Possession amount limits are far more about appeasing the fearful just to get legislation passed.

Summary: It's very likely it's being done to break the law (not guaranteed but likely). It's being done to close loopholes. There are similar (seemingly) stupid laws for alcohol (that are actually justified). In some cases alcohol is treated differently because it's less likely that it's being done to break the law.

Here's another way of looking at it. I can legally buy everything needed to build a fertilizer bomb (the type of bomb used in the Oklahoma City bombing). It's completely legal. It's essentially fertilizer and diesel fuel. I can legally drive around in, and park a moving truck full of diesel barrels anywhere I want. I can do the same with fertilizer. So therefore, I should legally be able to drive around and park anywhere a fertilizer bomb. And the cops can't do shit until I actually set it off, because maybe I don't plan on setting it off. Maybe I just want to express my freedom. I haven't committed a crime yet (and maybe I never will), so they shouldn't be able to do shit to me. Right? This is the logic used to limit pot purchases and possession. You're right, they maybe haven't committed a crime, maybe they never will.

But there actually are many similar laws with alcohol. Where I'm from you don't need to be driving to get charged with drinking and driving. The law says that "if you have the potential to drive drunk" the cops can charge you and you can be found guilty of drinking and driving without even driving! The reasons behind that are because they changed the law to erase all the bullshit loopholes truly guilty people have used to get out of it. And now because of people exposing and using loopholes the law has been changed to, "If a cop wants to completely fuck you over (even if you're completely innocent) they can". Which is the ONLY WAY to eliminate loopholes. So thank the people who have used loopholes, they're the reason laws like this exist.

So why can't you have as much pot as you want in your house? The answer is because "some people" will use it as a loophole in order to get away with committing a crime. Start making microbreweries and distillers that are as cheap, produce the same volume just as easily and at the same quality of intoxicants as can be produced with marijuana equipment, and there will be the same laws made for alcohol.

Why can someone have a shitload of wine and give it away? That wine's already been taxed (same with your cigarette question). Could someone have a shitload of illegally imported wine and disguise it as legal with the intent of illegally selling it? I guess, maybe. With pot you could be illegally importing it and disguising it as legally purchased very easily. I guess if illegal wine imports and sales became a big thing, similar laws would be passed for how much wine you could have.

Why can someone have a vineyard or fields of barley? It's still illegal to distill alcohol without a permit, even if it's for personal use. Marijuana doesn't need a step like that to become an intoxicant. Yes you can brew a certain amount of beer and make a certain amount of wine. If illegal wine and beer sales became a big enough problem there would be laws made. But right now you're still limited on how much you can brew.
